62c63a5c-e882-11f1-9238-a3575f438264.recap: Macro strategist Jim and vol/market-structure trader Noel (ex-Susquehanna floor trader, early GETCO backer) discuss their new partnership and a joint thesis: markets are governed by a 'three-legged stool' of structural options/flow positioning, macro fundamentals, and an unusually proactive administration's incentives. Jim argues the AI capex boom has been the sole pillar holding up an otherwise rolling-over economy, financed by massive hyperscaler debt issuance that is now crowding out sovereign debt; he cites CDS blowing out once the 10-year hit 5.3-5.4%, plus a wave of 2021 zero-rate debt needing refinancing. He expects the administration's incentive to support markets fades post-midterms, favoring a Fed-driven crisis/QE eventually, forecasting a 25-40% equity decline between February and June, likely as a grinding 'stair-step' lower rather than a correlation-to-one crash, given still-supportive year-end options flows (December OPEX) and heavy vol-compression/skew. They debate Fed credibility: Waller's floated 50bp hike is framed as 'Kabuki Theater' to preserve independence before an eventual dovish U-turn. They discuss curve dynamics (sticky long end despite rollover, volatile front end), trade ideas (VIX put spreads, gold calls/sell oil puts, steepener logic), and historical vol-compression-into-decline analogs (2015-16, 2018, 2022) warning that low realized vol during declines often precedes sharper drops. Much of the conversation centers on options/dispersion mechanics and reading dealer positioning.
terms: CDS -- credit default swap, a derivative providing protection against issuer default
OIS -- overnight index swap, used to derive risk-free short-term rate benchmarks
Vega -- an option's sensitivity to changes in implied volatility
Skew -- the difference in implied volatility across option strikes, reflecting relative demand for puts vs calls

e75e7439-30b7-4f25-b547-f9935b72ae5e.recap: Nouriel Roubini (ex-"Dr. Doom," now self-styled "Dr. Boom") and his Boom & Bust partner David Brown discuss how AI-driven technological innovation is, in Roubini's view, a first-order force that outweighs second-order risks like tariffs, geopolitics, and populism. He argues AI could lift US potential growth from ~2% to 4% by decade's end and much higher by 2040-50, funding redistribution to address rising inequality. Brown pushes back, framing the last 40 years as an unprecedented supply-side/low-rate boom now colliding with populism, deglobalization, and fiscal largesse — forces historically associated with structurally higher rates (citing 1970s inflation drivers). On rates specifically, Roubini argues nominal 10-year yields could stay near current levels by 2030, but the composition will shift: lower inflation offset by higher real rates driven by productivity-led growth, not fiscal distress. He dismisses Hank Paulson's "Treasury crisis" warning, arguing US yields are rising because of AI capex-driven private borrowing (a desirable, growth-driven dynamic) rather than inflation or fiscal panic, and that ample global private savings and equity financing will absorb issuance alongside hyperscaler debt-funded capex. He flags Meta's 30-year bonds yielding 7.5% as attractive given the durability of AI infrastructure. The conversation then shifts to David Brown's quantitative approach: using mean-reversion/standard-deviation signals plus Roubini's macro calls to time options (buying puts/gamma ahead of volatility clusters, e.g., February 2020) and portfolio sizing/cash discipline (~50% cash, selective leverage into selloffs).
